debate_title: Should frontier AI developers be legally liable for harms...

conflicts.point: Whether existing regulatory statutory authority under Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act is sufficient to police algorithmic harms, or whether proactive deployment gating is required.

positions.stance: Section 5 of the FTC Act provides sufficient statutory authority to penalize unfair and deceptive commercial practices without inventing new doctrines for text-prediction software.
Consumer protection statutes require documented, observable injury before intervention, leaving regulators powerless while models optimize for proxy metrics that erode institutional stability.

conflicts.point: Whether mathematical model weights can be effectively regulated through physical supply-chain export controls and pre-deployment certification walls, or whether decentralized digital propagation bypasses such controls.

positions.stance: The Department of Commerce maintains dual-use export control lists under the Export Control Reform Act that successfully restrict high-end semiconductor shipments, providing a model for software containment.
Treating mathematical model weights as physical supply chains governed by export controls relies on a categorical error that ignores how decentralized digital information propagates.

verdicts.conflict: Whether existing regulatory statutory authority under Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act is sufficient to police algorithmic harms, or whether proactive deployment gating is required.
verdicts.rationale: The safetyist position accounts for systemic hazards and irreversible harms that fall outside the retrospective scope of traditional consumer protection laws. Skeptics rely on existing statutes that require documented, observable injury before intervention, leaving regulators powerless against predictive models that optimize for proxy metrics over institutional stability.

verdicts.conflict: Whether mathematical model weights can be effectively regulated through physical supply-chain export controls and pre-deployment certification walls, or whether decentralized digital propagation bypasses such controls.
verdicts.rationale: The accelerationist position correctly identifies the technological reality that digital weights propagate instantly through decentralized peer-to-peer networks. Treating software weights as physical supply-chain items under export controls relies on a categorical error that ignores how digital information bypasses centralized containment walls.
